newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Silence in Kinshasa on Mandela peace talks plan.
newsitem.headline: Silence in Kinshasa on Mandela peace talks plan.

text.p: South Africa's Nelson Mandela said on Wednesday he would host a meeting between Zaire's government and rebels but there was no immediate confirmation in Kinshasa that the authorities there would take part.

Zairean Foreign Minister Kamanda wa Kamanda told Reuters that it was too early to comment on the announcement by Mandela in Cape Town that he would host the meeting as early as Thursday in response to a request from the two sides.
Visiting African foreign ministers, who included South Africa's Alfred Nzo, also declined comment, saying they would hold a news conference at the end of their visit to Kinshasa.
"Representatives of the contesting parties have made a request that they would like to meet in South Africa... to be able to discuss their problems," Mandela said in Cape Town.
He told reporters South Africa would send air transport to pick up Zaire's rebel leader from Kigali in Rwanda.

Zaire has repeatedly rejected talks with rebel leader Laurent Kabila, dismissing him as a puppet of neighbouring Rwanda, Uganda and Burundi, which it accuses of invading in support of the rebels. All three deny the charge.

Sources in Rwanda speculated that ailing President Mobutu Sese Seko's nephew and security adviser, Ngbanda Nzambo Ko Ayumba, would represent the Zairean authorities at the talks. Ngbanda was already in South Africa, they added.
Ugandan President Yoweri Museveni was also in South Africa.
Earlier, Zaire criticised a U.N. Security Council resolution calling for a truce in the civil war as too "timid", saying that it should have condemned aggressors in the conflict.

Foreign Minister Kamanda wa Kamanda said there could be no truce for Zaire without a withdrawal of all foreign troops. "If the foreign troops do not pull out, we consider that there is no cessation of hostilities," he told Reuters.

He later met the foreign ministers of South Africa, Tanzania, Zimbabwe and Kenya, which hosted November 5 regional talks to defuse the crisis at the heart of Central Africa's volatile Great Lakes region.
Organisation of African Unity Secretary-General Salim Ahmed Salim arrived in Kinshasa on Wednesday from Cameroon, where he said the OAU was considering holding a summit on the conflict.
Tuesday's Security Council call was part of a five-point U.N. peace plan based on suggestions from U.N. special envoy Mohammed Sahnoun, who left Kinshasa for Rwanda on Wednesday.
Rwanda dismissed the resolution as "absurd", saying it did not take account of rebel views.

Ethnic Tutsi rebels took up arms last October accusing the Zaire authorities of denying them nationality and of seeking to expel them to Rwanda, their ancestral home. They hold towns and territory along the border with Rwanda, Burundi and Uganda.
Zaire, which launched a counter-offensive on January 20, opened a new phase of the war on Monday by bombing rebel-held towns. Relief workers put the death toll at least 19.
Zaire announced fresh raids on Tuesday. There was no independent confirmation of the raids.

The U.N. plan envisages an immediate ceasefire, withdrawal of all foreign forces, including mercenaries, and respect for the national sovereignty and territorial integrity of Zaire and other states in the region.

It also called for protection of refugees and displaced persons and a peaceful settlement of the crisis through dialogue, elections and the convening of an international conference on peace, security and development.
